In [[algebraic K-theory]], a field of [[mathematics]], the '''Steinberg group''' <math> \operatorname{St}(A) </math> of a ring <math> A </math> is the [[universal central extension]] of the [[commutator subgroup]] of the stable [[general linear group]] of <math> A </math>.

It is named after [[Robert Steinberg]], and it is connected with [[Algebraic K-theory#Lower K-groups|lower <math> K </math>-groups]], notably <math> K_{2} </math> and <math> K_{3} </math>.

== Definition ==
Abstractly, given a ring <math> A </math>, the Steinberg group <math> \operatorname{St}(A) </math> is the [[universal central extension]] of the [[commutator subgroup]] of the [[stable general linear group]] (the commutator subgroup is perfect and so has a universal central extension).
=== Presentation using generators and relations ===

A concrete presentation using [[Presentation of a group|generators and relations]] is as follows. [[Elementary matrices]] — i.e. matrices of the form <math> {e_{pq}}(\lambda) := \mathbf{1} + {a_{pq}}(\lambda) </math>, where <math> \mathbf{1} </math> is the identity matrix, <math> {a_{pq}}(\lambda) </math> is the matrix with <math> \lambda </math> in the <math> (p,q) </math>-entry and zeros elsewhere, and <math> p \neq q </math> — satisfy the following relations, called the '''Steinberg relations''':
: <math>
\begin{align}
e_{ij}(\lambda) e_{ij}(\mu)                & = e_{ij}(\lambda+\mu);  && \\
\left[ e_{ij}(\lambda),e_{jk}(\mu) \right] & = e_{ik}(\lambda \mu),  && \text{for } i \neq k; \\
\left[ e_{ij}(\lambda),e_{kl}(\mu) \right] & = \mathbf{1},           && \text{for } i \neq l \text{ and } j \neq k.
\end{align}
</math>

The '''unstable Steinberg group''' of order <math> r </math> over <math> A </math>, denoted by <math> {\operatorname{St}_{r}}(A) </math>, is defined by the generators <math> {x_{ij}}(\lambda) </math>, where <math> 1 \leq i \neq j \leq r </math> and <math> \lambda \in A </math>, these generators being subject to the Steinberg relations. The '''stable Steinberg group''', denoted by <math> \operatorname{St}(A) </math>, is the [[direct limit]] of the system <math> {\operatorname{St}_{r}}(A) \to {\operatorname{St}_{r + 1}}(A) </math>. It can also be thought of as the Steinberg group of infinite order.

Mapping <math> {x_{ij}}(\lambda) \mapsto {e_{ij}}(\lambda) </math> yields a [[group homomorphism]] <math> \varphi: \operatorname{St}(A) \to {\operatorname{GL}_{\infty}}(A) </math>. As the elementary matrices generate the [[commutator subgroup]], this mapping is surjective onto the commutator subgroup.

=== Interpretation as a fundamental group ===
The Steinberg group is the [[fundamental group]] of the [[Volodin space]], which is the union of [[classifying space]]s of the [[unipotent]] subgroups of <math>\operatorname{GL}(A)</math>.

== Relation to ''K''-theory ==
=== ''K''<sub>1</sub> ===

<math> {K_{1}}(A) </math> is the [[cokernel]] of the map <math> \varphi: \operatorname{St}(A) \to {\operatorname{GL}_{\infty}}(A) </math>, as <math> K_{1} </math> is the abelianization of <math> {\operatorname{GL}_{\infty}}(A) </math> and the mapping <math> \varphi </math> is surjective onto the commutator subgroup.

=== ''K''<sub>2</sub> ===

<math> {K_{2}}(A) </math> is the [[centre (group theory)|center]] of the Steinberg group. This was Milnor's definition, and it also follows from more general definitions of higher <math> K </math>-groups.

It is also the kernel of the mapping <math> \varphi: \operatorname{St}(A) \to {\operatorname{GL}_{\infty}}(A) </math>. Indeed, there is an [[exact sequence]]
:<math> 1 \to {K_{2}}(A) \to \operatorname{St}(A) \to {\operatorname{GL}_{\infty}}(A) \to {K_{1}}(A) \to 1. </math>

Equivalently, it is the [[Schur multiplier]] of the group of [[elementary matrix|elementary matrices]], so it is also a [[homology group]]: <math> {K_{2}}(A) = {H_{2}}(E(A);\mathbb{Z}) </math>.

=== ''K''<sub>3</sub> ===

{{harvtxt|Gersten|1973}} showed that <math> {K_{3}}(A) = {H_{3}}(\operatorname{St}(A);\mathbb{Z}) </math>.
